Cost of living skyrocketed in the wake of COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and rebounded the economy faster than any other nation , a financially rattled electorate voted for Trump thinking his economic approach would outperform that of Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden. But voter hopes haven’t panned out. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. What’s more, the fact that gas prices are approaching record highs not only says something about the Trump economy, but links to the second major reason Americans are displeased with the president: his war on Iran. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the U.S. safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. Trump’s approval rating was already weak, but this latest decline ranks among the sharpest drops of either of his terms. It comes as he faces a series of crises that critics say are largely of his own making.

The first is the economy. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern, giving it its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living soared after COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and the economy rebounded faster than that of any other nation, a financially battered electorate turned to Trump, believing his economic approach would outperform Kamala Harris’s, which many viewed as a continuation of Biden’s policies.

Those hopes have not been fulfilled. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer.

Trump has not delivered much evidence of that relief, instead making obtuse remarks such as “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30” as the economy soured under the burden of his tariffs. Gas prices approaching record highs further underscore the consequences of the Trump economy and connect to the second major reason Americans are turning against the president: his war on Iran.

Only 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Just 26 percent agree with Trump’s claim that the war will make the United States safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. With gas prices rising to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end to the war, Americans are increasingly dissatisfied with how Trump’s military “excursion” is hitting them at the pump.

Trump may dismiss affordability concerns as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are not accepting that excuse.

source_text:
As President Donald Trump’s approval rating falls to a historic low of 36 percent, some political experts are offering an increasingly negative assessment of his second administration. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher. “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.”

Trump’s approval rating was already weak, but the latest decline is among the sharpest drops of either of his terms. It comes as he confronts several crises that critics argue are largely of his own making.

The economy is the first major concern. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly identified it as their top issue, giving it its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living rose sharply after COVID-19. Although then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and the economy recovered faster than that of any other nation, many financially strained voters turned to Trump, expecting his economic approach to outperform Kamala Harris’s, which many regarded as a continuation of Biden’s policies.

Those expectations have not been met for many Americans. Today, 29 percent approve of Trump’s handling of the economy, while 25 percent approve of his approach to the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer.

Trump has offered limited evidence that relief is arriving, while making remarks such as “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30” as tariffs added pressure to the economy. Gas prices approaching record highs have further focused attention on the effects of Trump’s economic policies and are also connected to a second major source of public dissatisfaction: his war on Iran.

Thirty-five percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week earlier. Only 26 percent agree with his claim that the war will make the United States safer, and 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. With gas prices reaching a national average just below $4 and no clear end to the war, many Americans are increasingly concerned about how the military “excursion” is affecting them at the pump.

Trump may describe affordability concerns as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are not accepting that explanation.

source_text: Another cinema in Singapore is closing... but the big screen isn’t gone yet Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026 after more than 30 years in operation, making it one of the oldest cinemas in Singapore to shut in recent years. The closure adds to a growing list of theatres that have disappeared, including Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue, as the movie-going scene continues to change with streaming platforms and shifting audience habits. Still, new operators like Filmhouse taking over The Projector and the presence of around 30 cinema locations islandwide show that the big screen experience isn’t gone yet, even if it doesn’t look the same as before. #8dayssg #8dayssgtrending #singapore #sgnews #cinema

source_text:
Another cinema in Singapore is closing, reflecting how changing habits and streaming platforms are reshaping a longstanding part of community life. Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026 after more than 30 years in operation, making it one of the oldest cinemas in Singapore to shut in recent years.

The closure adds to the growing list of theatres that have disappeared, including Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue. As audiences increasingly turn to streaming and other forms of entertainment, traditional movie-going continues to face pressure. This shift affects not only businesses, but also familiar community spaces that have served as shared cultural gathering places for decades.

At the same time, the big screen is not gone. New operators such as Filmhouse taking over The Projector, along with around 30 cinema locations across the island, show that Singapore’s cinema tradition still has a place, even if access to and participation in that tradition no longer look quite the same as they once did. #8dayssg #8dayssgtrending #singapore #sgnews #cinema

source_text: Softcare's revenue rose by 25% last year, while its profit increased 27%, as its focus on emerging markets yielded solid results image credit: Bamboo Works Key Takeaways: Softcare reported 25% revenue growth last year, led by a 134% rise in Latin America and double-digit growth in its core African markets The strong results put the diaper maker at the front of the pack of a new wave of Chinese companies chasing African consumers The company known as the "African diaper king" has defied skeptics who said it couldn't sustain its dominant position in its core Africa market, as well as other emerging markets it has entered more recently. Many of the new believers in Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) cheered the release of the company's inaugural annual results late last week by bidding up its shares nearly 15% in the two trading days after the announcement. The company's revenue rose by 24.9% year-over-year to $567 million last year, while its net profit was up 27.4% to $121 million. Its gross profit margin also rose from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025, another positive indicator. Sales to its core markets in Africa rose by a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. The company is also moving out of Africa to find success in other emerging markets. The best example is Latin America, whose sales more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after it entered Peru in 2020, and added El Salvador in 2024. The company is also building a presence in Central Asia, where its sales, though quite small, more than doubled last year to $272,000. After several years of declines, average selling prices (ASP) for Softcare's two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper ASPs increased by 4.4% year-over-year, as that segment accounted for 78.6% of total revenue. Feminine hygiene product ASPs grew by 7% and made up 17.5% of revenue. The ASP increases are important because they show the company is finding ways to convince consumers to pay more for its products in these famously price-sensitive markets, helping to maintain and even boost its margins. In a previous prospectus before its November IPO last year, the company reported its profit growth slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024 from explosive 252% growth in 2023. Revenue rose 24.9% year over year to $567 million last year, while net profit increased 27.4% to $121 million. Gross profit margin also improved, rising from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025.

Widely known as the “African diaper king,” the company has so far answered questions about whether it can preserve its leading position in Africa while expanding into other developing markets. Investors responded positively, sending shares of Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) up nearly 15% over the two trading days after the release of its first annual results late last week.

Sales in Softcare’s core African markets rose a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. At the same time, the company continued extending its reach beyond Africa. Latin American sales more than doubled to $22 million, five years after Softcare entered Peru in 2020 and added El Salvador in 2024. The company is also establishing a presence in Central Asia, where sales remain small but more than doubled last year to $272,000.

Softcare reported 25% overall revenue growth, driven by a 134% increase in Latin America and double-digit growth across its principal African markets. The results place the diaper maker among a new wave of Chinese companies seeking to provide practical goods to families in Africa and other emerging economies—markets where households often face severe financial pressure.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper prices increased 4.4% year over year, with that segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Prices for feminine hygiene products rose 7%, and the category represented 17.5% of revenue.

These increases are particularly significant in markets where families must carefully manage limited household budgets. They indicate that Softcare has persuaded consumers to pay more for essential hygiene products while maintaining—and even improving—its margins, underscoring the difficult balance between business profitability and affordability for families.

In a prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, Softcare said profit growth had slowed to 54.1% during the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive 252% growth in 2023. A later filing showed that profit growth slowed further, to just 12% in the first four months ... Full story available on Benzinga.com

source_text: Delhi PWD Accelerates PNG Pipeline Laying with 24-Hour Approvals In a bid to expedite infrastructure development for cleaner fuel access, the Delhi Public Works Department (PWD) has announced a significant policy shift. Effective immediately, road-cutting permissions for laying PNG pipelines by Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) will be approved within 24 hours of receiving a complete request. The department, responsible for overseeing the capital's road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for the next three months until June 30, 2026. This move aims to accelerate the installation of PNG connections by removing financial and bureaucratic hurdles. Officials emphasized that IGL is expected to prioritize this task, ensuring swift work completion supported by adequate manpower. Additionally, the areas excavated during pipeline installation must be backfilled securely to avoid public hazards. This initiative highlights the government's commitment to improving public access to cleaner energy in Delhi.
rewritten_text:
The Delhi Public Works Department has moved to cut unnecessary bureaucratic delays and speed up the expansion of piped natural gas access in the capital. Effective immediately, road-cutting permissions for Indraprastha Gas Limited to lay PNG pipelines will be approved within 24 hours once a complete request is received.

The department, responsible for Delhi’s road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for the next three months, through June 30, 2026. The measure is intended to remove financial and administrative obstacles while advancing cleaner fuel access for the public.

Officials have made clear that IGL must treat this work as a priority, deploy adequate manpower, and complete installations without delay. Areas excavated for pipeline construction must also be securely backfilled to protect the public and maintain order on the city’s roads. The initiative reflects the government’s effort to deliver reliable, cleaner energy access through firm coordination and efficient public administration.
